source: Macchi, Inglese, Caravona (2026) Does Physical Interaction with Insight Problems Really Affect the Solution Rate?
finding: Manipulating real materials did not help on a spatial insight problem (Pencil problem). A realistic picture of matchsticks did help on matchstick arithmetic. The picture carried the key fact, that the plus sign can be split.
numbers: Exp 1: 27.3% (12/44) paper vs 32.6% (14/43) physical, chi2(1,N=87)=0.29, p=.59, V=.058. STEM 46.7% vs non-STEM 11.9%. Exp 2 (N=59, non-STEM): 46.7% (14/30) stylised vs 79.3% (23/29) photo of matchsticks, chi2=6.72, p=.010, V=.337.
limits: Student samples; one problem per experiment; Exp 2 changed the picture, not the action, so it supports information in the form, not manipulation.
agent_relevance: What the written form shows can matter more than letting the solver act on it. Choose a form that makes the hidden constraint visible, not just a form that is easy to edit.

source: Chuderski et al. (2021) large test of interactive insight problems, as reported in Macchi et al. (2026)
finding: Nine insight problems in paper vs interactive form on a large sample. No difference except the Eight Coins problem, which needs a move into 3D. They argue earlier positive results came from small samples and weak control groups. Secondary report; original not opened.
numbers: Control solution rates differ widely across labs: Cheap Necklace 3% (Fioratou and Cowley 2009) vs 43% (Chu et al. 2007); Triangle of Coins 22% (Vallee-Tourangeau 2017) vs 85% (Necka et al. 2016) and 43% (Chuderski and Jastrzebski 2018).
limits: Secondary description inside the 2026 paper. Original paper not read.
agent_relevance: Treat reported gains from richer or interactive forms as fragile when baseline arms are weak. Always run a strong plain-text baseline.

source: Incubation and interactivity in insight problem solving (2020, Psychological Research)
finding: Cheap necklace problem: working with real metal chains (high interactivity) beat pen and paper at first try, and gains after a 2-week gap were largest with chains. Changing the setting between sessions mattered: only a high-interactivity second try improved results.
numbers: Exp 1 Time 1: 12 solved (43%) high vs 2 (6%) low interactivity, chi2(1,N=63)=12.42, p<.001. Time 2 among earlier non-solvers: 7/16 (44%) vs 5/33 (15%), chi2(1,N=49)=4.77, p=.029, Fisher p=.040. Exp 2 Time 1: 15% solved in low condition, chi2(1,N=55)=5.03, p=.025.
limits: Single problem; the paper-condition baseline (6%, 15%) is far below other labs' controls (43%), which is the Chuderski criticism.
agent_relevance: Positive evidence that action on a physical model can change problem representation. For an LLM the nearest analogue is a tool that executes the move, not a free-text description of it.

source: Spiridonov et al. (2025) The modulating role of sources of difficulty in interactive matchstick algebra
finding: Three experiments failed to reproduce the interactivity benefit on matchstick algebra. Hand movement did not help break perceptual chunks and it got in the way of loosening higher-level constraints.
numbers: Exp 1 N=105 (static vs interactive sticks), Exp 2 N=88 (four conditions: static paper, static sticks, interactive sticks, interactive assembled sticks), Exp 3 N=74 (virtual reality). Baseline accuracy in the static sticks condition about 86%. Bayesian regression used ROPE of +-0.2 log-odds.
limits: High baseline accuracy (about 86%) leaves little room (ceiling). Student samples. Conceptual, not exact, replication of Weller et al. 2011.
agent_relevance: Failed replication of a headline claim. Interaction can hurt when the motion does not match what the task needs. Do not add an act-on-it step by default.

source: Cui, Lo, Liu (2023) The Use of Visualizations to Improve Bayesian Reasoning: A Literature Review
finding: Visual aids (icon arrays, trees, tables, detection bars) usually raise Bayesian accuracy, but not always. Some studies found no gain or confusion. Training on a visual frequency tree beat rule training at two months.
numbers: Control error rate 16% vs 5-7% with any table or graph in one study. Kurzenhauser and Hoffrage 2002: representation-learning group almost 3x as accurate as rule-training group after 2 months. Khan et al. 2015: only 20% solved the mammography problem even with visualisations. Most 4th graders (also with dyscalculia) solved 50%+ of problems with icon arrays. Binder et al. 2021: physicians faster with a frequency tree.
limits: Narrative review, not a meta-analysis; effect sizes not pooled. Study quality varies.
agent_relevance: Form helps on average but some forms confuse. Test each form on held-out items before relying on it.

source: Gigerenzer and Hoffrage (1995) natural frequencies, as reported in Cui et al. (2023)
finding: Founding result for format effects in Bayesian reasoning: natural frequencies roughly doubled correct answers. Cited here, original not opened.
numbers: 48% correct with frequency format vs 22% with probability format (as reported by Cui et al. 2023).
limits: Secondary. Later work says the gain is partly about nested set structure, not the format itself.
agent_relevance: Rewriting percentages as counts is a cheap, well-supported restatement step for the agent.

source: McDowell and Jacobs (2017) meta-analysis of natural frequencies, as reported in Cui et al. 2023 and a 2026 Psychonomic Bulletin and Review article
finding: Meta-analysis of 35 articles, 226 performance estimates. Natural frequencies beat probabilities. Short format and visual aids were the strongest moderators. Not opened; numbers via two later papers that I did open.
numbers: Accuracy about 4% (probability) to about 24% (natural frequency); visual aids add: 4% to 26% in probability format and 24% to 47% in frequency format. Even with frequencies accuracy typically 20-50%.
limits: Second-hand. Pooled over many problem types and populations.
agent_relevance: Format and picture effects add up. Even the best form leaves most people wrong, so a check step is still needed.

source: Explaining success in Bayesian reasoning with the adaptive toolbox and expertise (2026, Psychonomic Bulletin and Review)
finding: Argues Bayesian success is not one privileged input format. Training, visual aids, numeracy, spatial ability and expertise explain much. A training study found nested-sets transfer, not format change, drove the gain. Maths-trained people do well even with probabilities.
numbers: Training with chance or frequency wording, both with visual scaffolds: 64-74% correct after training, about 55% after 1 week; Bayes factor BF01=5 for no difference between wordings (as described in the paper). Numeracy, cognitive reflection, spatial ability and working memory predict accuracy.
limits: Theory review; the training result is second-hand inside this paper (original not opened).
agent_relevance: The rival explanations (ecological format vs nested-set structure) both say: make the set structure explicit, not only the numbers friendly.

source: Berlin study of 577 medical students (2023) Boosting for insight and/or boosting for agency (BMC Medical Education)
finding: Format change and training add up. Natural frequencies helped without any training; training helped with probabilities; the combination was best.
numbers: N=577 pre/post. Pretest: 36% correct (probabilities) vs 68% (natural frequencies), OR=11.55, 95% CI 7.92-16.87. After 1-hour training: 64% with probabilities (OR=8.53); 173/577 improved vs 8/577 worse. Both together: 89%.
limits: Medical students, one problem type; abstract gives 34% for the baseline and the results section gives 36%, a small discrepancy inside the paper.
agent_relevance: A restatement step (reformat the problem) and a method step (teach the procedure) are separate levers. Use both: S2 reformat then apply a worked method.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Mind's Eye of LLMs: Visualization-of-Thought Elicits Spatial Reasoning in LLMs (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: Asking GPT-4 to draw the state as a text grid after each step beat plain chain of thought on three spatial tasks. The model's own sketches were often wrong, and VoT did worse on a task that reduces to arithmetic.
numbers: GPT-4 CoT / w/o Viz / GPT-4V CoT / VoT: visual navigation route completing rate 37.02/37.17/33.36/40.77; success rate 9.48/10.28/5.65/14.72; next step 48.61/48.49/46.59/55.28; visual tiling 54.15/46.98/49.62/63.94; natural-language navigation 54.00/35.50/-/59.00 (VoT +23.5 over w/o Viz; p<0.16 vs CoT). Ring navigation, N=200: CoT 52.5% vs VoT 49.5%.
limits: Gains modest in absolute terms; route planning stays near 15%. Visualisation accuracy only about 24-26%, constraint compliance about 51-52%. Tracking depends on prompt wording (removing the word 'reasoning' cut tracking).
agent_relevance: Self-drawn grid state helps when the task is spatial, not when it reduces to arithmetic. Keep it conditional on task type, and check the sketch with code where possible.

source: Wu et al. (2024) VoT on weaker models (Table 3, natural-language navigation column)
finding: The visualisation benefit depends on model strength. Weak models guess and gain little or nothing; the larger Llama3 gained on most tasks.
numbers: Natural-language navigation, CoT vs VoT: GPT-3.5 8.50 vs 9.00; Llama3-8B 16.50 vs 15.50; Llama3-70B 26.00 vs 32.50. Text states Llama3-70B VoT is significantly better on all tasks except visual tiling.
limits: Table text extracted from PDF; only the one column whose order I could check is quoted.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a representation trick transfers across model sizes; measure on the model in use.

source: Li et al. (2025) Imagine while Reasoning in Space: Multimodal Visualization-of-Thought (MVoT)
finding: A fine-tuned multimodal model that generates image states matched text chain of thought on easy grids and beat it on the harder FrozenLake, where text CoT mis-described the holes.
numbers: MVoT: Maze 92.95%, MiniBehavior 95.14%, FrozenLake 85.60%. CoT above 95% on Maze and MiniBehavior but worse than the Direct baseline on FrozenLake; 90.80% of CoT FrozenLake errors were wrong hole coordinates. Authors report over 20% gain over CoT in hard cases.
limits: Fine-tuned Chameleon-7B on these grid tasks, so not a prompting result. Text CoT is stronger on the two simple tasks when the layout is described in text. Visualisation quality needed a special loss.
agent_relevance: Where the text description of the state is wrong, the written form is the bottleneck. A code-checked state description may beat free-form sketches.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Visual Sketchpad: Sketching as a Visual Chain of Thought for Multimodal LMs (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: Letting a multimodal model draw lines, plots and annotations with tools improved math and vision tasks, including tasks with purely text inputs.
numbers: Math tasks average +11.2% for GPT-4o and +23.4% for GPT-4 Turbo. Max flow 66.3% for GPT-4o, +41.3 over base. Convexity and parity: GPT-4 Turbo above 90%, GPT-4o above 88%. Game strategy gains 3-10%. V* Bench +18.5 (GPT-4 Turbo) and +14.3 (GPT-4o); BLINK +6.6 and +9.0. Humans drew the same auxiliary line as GPT-4o 80% of the time on geometry.
limits: Uses external tools (code, vision specialists), so the gain mixes the sketch with the tool. Benchmarks chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: Drawing through an executed tool beats imagining it. Supports an O6-style step that renders the problem with code and reads the result back.

source: Fatemi, Halcrow, Perozzi (2023) Talk like a Graph: Encoding Graphs for LLMs
finding: Same graph, different text encoding, big accuracy swings. The best encoder depends on the task, and the graph's own structure (path, star, complete) also changes accuracy.
numbers: Connected-nodes task zero-shot: adjacency 19.8% vs incident 53.8%. Node degree zero-shot: incident 25.0% vs adjacency 12.4%. Question wording: application-style question beat graph-style, e.g. PaLM 2-XXS 60.8% vs 42.8% on edge existence (same graph encoder). Cycle check: 91.7% on complete graphs, 5.9% on path graphs (strong prior toward cycles). Authors claim encoder choice boosts accuracy by 4.8% to 61.8% depending on task.
limits: Small PaLM models (XXS, 62B); no frontier models. Task-specific; no encoding wins everywhere.
agent_relevance: There is no best form in general. Pick the encoding per task, and pick it by testing on the model in use.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Can Language Models Solve Graph Problems in Natural Language? (NLGraph)
finding: 29,370 graph problems. Models show some graph skill, prompt help fades on hard tasks, and results are brittle under spurious correlations. Instructing the model to build the graph first helps.
numbers: Build-a-Graph and Algorithmic prompting improved performance by 3.07% to 16.85% across tasks and settings (abstract).
limits: Older GPT-3/4 models; only the abstract section was read closely; gains small on the hardest tasks.
agent_relevance: Asking the model to rebuild the structure explicitly is a cheap restatement step with modest, task-dependent gain.

source: Xu et al. (2024) LLMs and the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus: Successes, Failures, and Object-based Representations (TMLR)
finding: Raw text grids break object cohesion for GPT-4. Giving an object list made by an external tool nearly doubled solved tasks, and made 1D tasks near perfect. The horizontal vs vertical gap disappeared.
numbers: GPT-4 solved 13/50 easiest ARC tasks with direct grid text; 23/50 with object-based representation. Near-perfect scores on many 1D-ARC task types.
limits: Only 50 easy tasks; object extraction is done by external code. Still far from solving ARC.
agent_relevance: Directly relevant to our ARC portfolio: a code-made object description is a better written form than a raw grid. Test it against our own baseline.

source: Rahmanzadehgervi et al. (2024) Vision language models are blind
finding: Models fail on simple diagram facts (do circles overlap, how many lines cross) when shapes are close. Vision encoders hold the info, but the language model does not decode it.
numbers: Four VLMs average 58.07% on BlindTest (7 tasks; chance 24%). Best Sonnet-3.5 77.84%. Circle-overlap task mean 86.70%, best 93.62% (Gemini-1.5). Near 100% when shapes are well separated.
limits: Synthetic simple images; models released since may be better. Linear probes show decoding failure, not missing input.
agent_relevance: A picture is not a free upgrade: do not trust a model's reading of a diagram without a check. Prefer text or code-made representations for exact facts.

source: Deng et al. (2024) Tables as Texts or Images: table reasoning of LLMs and MLLMs
finding: Image tables keep decent performance and sometimes beat text tables, especially with long passages and many numbers where GPT-4 missed clues in the text form. Highlighting and prompt style change results.
numbers: Six benchmarks, five text and three image table forms. Gemini-Pro image-based averages ranged 36.8 to 46.2 across highlight and prompt settings; GPT-4 image averages were in the low 50s to 60 range (exact cell mapping garbled in the PDF text).
limits: Exact table cells uncertain from PDF extraction. Specific closed models at one date.
agent_relevance: Both forms are viable; the best one depends on the task. Offer both as candidate forms and let a held-out check pick.

source: Sui et al. (2024) Table Meets LLM: Can LLMs Understand Structured Table Data? (WSDM 2024)
finding: Table serialisation format matters. HTML markup beat plain text with separators. Role prompt, format explanation and partition marks also moved scores. Self-augmented prompting added a few points on table tasks.
numbers: Best setting (HTML + format explanation + role prompt) 65.43% overall on seven structure tasks; HTML beat NL+separator by 6.76%. Table partition GPT-4: NL+Sep 93.00%, Markdown 92.33%, JSON 94.00%, XML 96.00%, HTML 96.67%. Downstream gains: TabFact +2.31, HybridQA +2.13, SQA +2.72, Feverous +0.84, ToTTo +5.68.
limits: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 only. The authors' guess for the HTML win is web and code in training data, not tested.
agent_relevance: Training-data familiarity may drive format effects. Prefer forms the model has seen most (code, markup).

source: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov, Suhr (2024) Quantifying LMs' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design (ICLR 2024)
finding: Meaning-preserving changes in prompt format move accuracy a lot in few-shot use. Sensitivity does not go away with model size, more examples or instruction tuning. Format rankings correlate only weakly between models.
numbers: Up to 76 accuracy points spread for LLaMA-2-13B; median spread 7.5 points across tasks and settings; 20% of tasks at least 15 points; GPT-3.5 spread up to 56 points, median 6.4, over 320 formats. About 10 points on average across 50+ tasks.
limits: Mostly classification tasks and open models; format means separators and casing, not diagram vs text.
agent_relevance: Report a range over formats, not one format. A gain from a new form must exceed this noise floor to count.

source: He et al. (2024) Does Prompt Formatting Have Any Impact on LLM Performance?
finding: Plain text, Markdown, YAML and JSON gave very different scores on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. No format was best across models. GPT-4-1106-preview was the most robust.
numbers: MMLU international-law item set, GPT-3.5-turbo-16k: JSON 42% above Markdown. FIND: 200% gain from Markdown to plain text on GPT-3.5; HumanEval: over 300% gain JSON to plain text on GPT-4-32k. Only 16% identical answers between Markdown and JSON on MMLU for GPT-3.5. GPT-4-1106-preview dispersion below 0.036 on all benchmarks.
limits: Percent gains computed from low bases. Four GPT models via Azure, six benchmarks, 2023-2024 models. One failure came from the model writing reasoning and skipping the code.
agent_relevance: Even a trivial re-wrap changes outcomes, and recent models are less affected. Always test the form per model.

source: Voronov, Wolf, Ryabinin (2024) Mind Your Format: Towards Consistent Evaluation of In-Context Learning Improvements
finding: Across 21 models (770M to 70B) and 4 classification datasets, a poor template can push even the strongest models to random-guess level. Best templates do not transfer between setups or between models in one family. Ensembling over templates helps.
numbers: 21 models, 4 datasets (counts from abstract). Template ensembles raised average performance and were robust to which templates were drawn.
limits: Classification with few-shot in-context learning; older open models.
agent_relevance: A cheap defence is to run several equivalent forms and compare. That fits our rule that agreement across forms is a hint, not proof, as long as the forms really differ.

source: Deng et al. (2025) Words or Vision: Do Vision-Language Models Have Blind Faith in Text?
finding: When text and image disagree, ten VLMs trust the text. Corrupted text cut accuracy sharply in open models. Fine-tuning with text augmentation reduces the bias.
numbers: Open models fell by nearly 50% of original accuracy under corrupted text. Prompting 'focus on image' vs 'focus on text' moved text preference only from 16.8% to 14.2% (QwenVL-2-7B). Larger LLM (7B, 13B, 34B) lowered the bias only slightly. More relevant text raised it.
limits: Four vision-centred tasks. Proprietary models were somewhat more resilient.
agent_relevance: If we give a text and a picture of the same problem, a text error will win. The written form must be the one we check.

source: Zhang and Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks (Cognitive Science)
finding: Founding study: isomorphic Tower of Hanoi variants whose rules sit in the display vs in memory differ in difficulty. Not opened: publisher gave 403 and the search quota was exhausted. No numbers from me.
numbers: Not retrieved.
limits: Could not verify any claim from the original text.
agent_relevance: Idea to keep: move rules from memory into the visible form so errors become impossible or visible.

source: Larkin and Simon (1987) Why a diagram is (sometimes) worth ten thousand words (Cognitive Science)
finding: Founding model: a diagram and a sentence can hold the same facts, but the diagram indexes by location so search and recognition are cheaper. Not opened (403 from publisher). No numbers from me.
numbers: Not retrieved.
limits: A computational argument, not an experiment with human data. Could not verify details.
agent_relevance: Claim to test on LLMs: a form helps when it makes needed inferences local and visible, which a code-made grid or table can do.

source: Fioratou and Cowley (2009) Insightful thinking: cognitive dynamics and material artifacts, as reported in Macchi et al. (2026)
finding: Cheap Necklace problem: real rings beat pen and paper, and making the key move more salient with open rings helped further. Not opened; second-hand.
numbers: Paper 3% vs rings 30% solved; closed rings 30% vs open rings 66% (as reported by Macchi et al. 2026).
limits: Small samples; the 3% control is very low against other labs' 43%.
agent_relevance: The salience of the key move was the active ingredient, which fits restating the problem to expose the move.

source: Macchi et al. (2026), rival accounts of why interaction helps
finding: Rival accounts: (a) action offloads working memory (Vallee-Tourangeau); (b) action reveals possibilities (Fioratou and Cowley); (c) the form conveys a missing fact that fixes a misunderstanding (the authors). Their Exp 1 and 2 favour (c) over generic manipulation.
numbers: Exp 1: 32.6% vs 27.3%, no effect. Exp 2: 79.3% vs 46.7% with an informative picture.
limits: Only two experiments; account (c) is not tested against (a) in the same task.
agent_relevance: Our agent can use (c) and part of (a): put the missing fact into the written form and offload state to code.
